His father is an official of the Sardinian crown and a doctor of law, and whatever fortune the marriage brought is already going into speculations that will not come back. stops.campa: He enrolls at about fourteen to read law, which is his father's wish, and reads it without appetite. What turns him is a copy of Halley's 1693 paper on the use of algebra in optics. After that he works through Newton, Leibniz, the Bernoullis, Euler and Clairaut on his own, in no order anyone set for him. The mathematics of the century reaches him as reading rather than as teaching. Nobody examines him in it, nobody directs it, and nobody in Turin is far enough ahead of him to say whether he is getting it right. By 1752 the law is finished.

stops.campa: On the twelfth of August he writes to Leonhard Euler in Berlin with his results on the tautochrone and with a purely analytic method for problems of maxima and minima, one that throws away the geometrical constructions Euler himself had used to get the equation in 1744. Euler reads a letter from a nineteen-year-old in Turin, understands at once what it is, and holds back his own account so the younger man will have the credit for the method. The calculus of variations starts in this exchange and takes its name from Euler.

No diagrams will be found in this work. Those who love Analysis will see with pleasure that Mechanics has become a branch of it, and will be grateful to me for having thus extended its domain.

stops.campa: He dies at home on the tenth of April, seventy-seven years old, in the western faubourgs of a city he first entered fifty years earlier as a sick young man travelling on another man's ambassadorial passage. He had been an academician of Berlin at twenty, a director of mathematics at thirty, and a professor for the first time at fifty-eight. The second volume of the Mécanique analytique is on the desk, half of it written. Other hands complete it and print it in 1815.

stops.campa: He is given a solemn funeral and laid in the crypt of the Panthéon, vault two, among the great men of a nation he was born a foreigner to. The inscription cut for him is a list of what four regimes made of him and of the two cities that bracket it: senator, count of the Empire, grand officer of the Legion of Honour, grand cross of the Imperial Order of the Reunion, member of the Institute and of the Bureau of Longitude, born at Turin, died at Paris.
stops.quote: Lagrange is the lofty pyramid of the mathematical sciences.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Napoleon. [R]: Luigi Pepe, 'Lagrange (1736-1813): a life in mathematics', Lettera Matematica 2 (2014), 3-8, reports that Napoleon defined him as la haute pyramide des sciences mathématiques; the phrase was popularised in English by E. T. Bell, Men of Mathematics (1937), whose Lagrange chapter is titled 'The Lofty Pyramid'. No contemporaneous speech, letter or Moniteur report was located, and neither Wikiquote nor the MacTutor quotations archive carries it.

stops.name: Paris, the two eulogies and the fourteen volumes
stops.date_confidence: two things at one pin. Treccani records the immediate commemoration on both sides of the Alps, Delambre's notice read at the Institut in Paris and Antonio Maria Vassalli Eandi's in Turin, both in 1813, and gives the Oeuvres de Lagrange edited by J.-A. Serret and G. Darboux, 14 volumes, Paris, 1867-1892. The stop is dated to the first volume of the edition and the eulogies of 1813 are carried in the campa rather than given a stop of their own; months are not recorded. The 1997 Kluwer translation of the second edition by Boissonnade and Vagliente is from en.wikipedia's article on the Mécanique analytique. Institut pin 48.8566, 2.3376 inherited byte-identical from pierre_simon_laplace.journey.json, which is the quai Conti building the Institut occupied from 1805.
stops.campa: Delambre reads the memorial notice at the Institut, and in Turin, Antonio Maria Vassalli Eandi commemorates him before the academy that began as three young men reading papers to each other in 1757. Half a century later Joseph-Alfred Serret and Gaston Darboux gather the whole of it into fourteen volumes: the Turin memoirs, the Berlin memoirs, the Paris memoirs, the prize essays, the letters. The calculus of variations he began at nineteen has a name and a literature by then. The printing runs in Paris from 1867 to 1892, twenty-five years of it.

stops.name: The Eiffel Tower, the sixth name on the north-west face
stops.date_confidence: attested that Lagrange is among the 72 names inscribed on the Eiffel Tower and that his stands sixth on the north-west face, which looks toward the Trocadéro, per en.wikipedia's list. The tower was completed in 1889; the month of the inscription is not recorded and defaults to 1 January. The letter height of about sixty centimetres is from the same list article. That Lavoisier, Monge, Laplace, Fourier, Poisson and Cauchy are also on the frieze is checkable on the same list; all six have direct documented relations to Lagrange recorded elsewhere in this file. Pin 48.8583, 2.2945 inherited byte-identical from joseph_fourier.journey.json, stop 'Paris, the name on the Eiffel Tower'; the research pool gave 48.8584, 2.2945 and the corpus pair is preferred.
stops.campa: Seventy-six years after his death France cuts seventy-two names of scientists and engineers into the frieze of the tower on the Champ de Mars. He shares the ironwork with Lavoisier, Monge, Laplace, Fourier, Poisson and Cauchy: most of the commission that made the metre, and most of the men who sat in the rooms where he lectured. His own name stands sixth on the north-west face, the side that looks toward the Trocadéro, in gilt letters about sixty centimetres high.

stops.name: Turin, via Lagrange and the five points
stops.date_confidence: the date is an ordering device only: no source reached gives a year for the naming of via Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange in Turin. Coordinate corrected against the research pool, which gave 45.068, 7.685, about 350 m east of the street; Nominatim centres via Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange, Torino at 45.0629, 7.6806. The lunar crater Lagrange and asteroid (1006) Lagrangea are from en.wikipedia's legacy section; the Lagrange points and their modern use in astrodynamics are from fr.wikipedia and NASA Science. Rue Lagrange in the fifth arrondissement of Paris, at approximately 48.8515, 2.3480, is a second street of the same name and is not given a stop of its own.
stops.campa: In the centre of the city he left at thirty a street carries his name in the Italian form the baptismal register gave him, not the French form Europe reads. A crater on the Moon is called Lagrange, and so is an asteroid, 1006 Lagrangea. In Paris a street in the fifth arrondissement, near Notre-Dame, carries it too. The five equilibrium points of the three-body problem, three of them Euler's and two of them found on paper in Berlin in 1772, are called the Lagrange points and are used to park real machines in real orbits.

stops.name: Mont Gros, Nice: the Laboratoire Lagrange
stops.date_confidence: the Laboratoire Lagrange, UMR 7293, jointly run by the CNRS, the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur and the Université Côte d'Azur on the Mont Gros site above Nice, is recorded in fr.wikipedia's honors section for Lagrange. The founding year of the unit was not established by anything reached and 2011 is a placed value to order the stop, not a source date; the research areas named in the campa are the laboratory's own standing description and were not refetched. Coordinate 43.7237, 7.2975 is the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, Mont Gros, from the research pool's afterlife lens; it is not a corpus-canonical pin. He never went to Nice, and the stop is an afterlife stop for the name, not a scene.
stops.campa: On the Mont Gros above Nice a laboratory of the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur carries his name, a joint unit of the CNRS and the university. Its people work on the formation of planets, on stellar physics, and on the mechanics of many bodies pulling on one another, which is the problem the Paris Academy set him in 1764 and again in 1772. Those questions are still open on this hill, asked now of systems around other stars rather than of the Moon and of Jupiter's four satellites. He never came to this coast.
suggested_refs: Laboratoire Lagrange, UMR 7293, Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur
